## Implementation notes

### ACE-Step (`acestep`)

`ace-server` exposes an asynchronous job API: `POST /lm` or `POST /synth` returns a job id immediately, `GET /job?id=N` polls the status, and `GET /job?id=N&result=1` fetches the finished result. `AceStepServer::run_job` wraps this submit/poll/fetch cycle with a ceiling of roughly 20 minutes per stage at a 1-second poll cadence. Synth results arrive as `multipart/mixed` (an audio part plus a latent part); Lemonade extracts the first audio part.

Vocals are a two-stage pipeline. `POST /lm` with `lm_mode: "generate"` runs the ACE-Step language model, which turns the caption and lyrics into audio codes plus LM-filled metadata, returned as a JSON array of enriched requests. That array is accepted by `POST /synth` verbatim, so Lemonade feeds it through unchanged. `POST /synth` on its own is the DiT-only instrumental path — it has no language model and cannot sing, so a `lyrics` value (other than the sentinel below) is what routes a request through `/lm` first.

`[Instrumental]` — any case, surrounding whitespace ignored — is ACE-Step's sentinel for the no-vocals path, matching the Python reference implementation. Instrumental requests send the sentinel explicitly rather than an empty string because the synth stage also feeds the lyrics text into its conditioning.

Errors from `audio_generations` are written into the response sink as a JSON error payload; the endpoint handler turns that into an HTTP error instead of shipping it as audio.

The model download fetches the DiT checkpoint variant plus three companions when present in the repo: the language model (`acestep-5Hz-lm-4B-Q8_0.gguf`, required for vocals and auto-lyrics), the Qwen3 text encoder, and the VAE. The checkpoint path handed to `--models` is the directory of GGUFs; `ace-server` scans it by architecture, and `--keep-loaded` keeps models resident across requests.

### Gufo (`gufo`)

Gufo is a vertical inference engine built for AMD Strix Halo (`gfx1151`); the support row is Linux + `gfx1151` only and there is no fallback — on any other host the recipe is inert. Upstream publishes no standalone binaries, so the backend is **system-managed**: it resolves the executable from the `gufo.server_bin` config key or `LEMONADE_GUFO_SERVER_BIN` env var, falling back to `gufo` on `PATH`. `lemonade backends install gufo` refuses with that remediation instead of downloading. The container image is the exception: the root `Dockerfile` builds the engine from the pinned upstream tag (`ARG GUFO_VERSION`) in a `gufo-builder` stage against the ROCm 7.2 apt repository and installs it as `/usr/local/bin/gufo`, where plain PATH resolution finds it. Building by hand needs the stock AMD ROCm 7.2 runtime; on Ubuntu the distro gcc builds cleanly (the private GCC 15 toolchain was only needed to dodge GCC 16's `__noinline__`/`<format>` clash on Arch hosts). gufo is deliberately **not** a TheRock recipe.

`gufo serve <modality>` serves exactly one model and one modality per process, so `GufoServer::load()` picks the subcommand (`llm`/`asr`/`tts`/`image`) from the model's deployment mode. The listener binds only after weights are resident, so `/health` success already means model-ready. `--served-model-name` is set to the Lemonade model id because gufo 404s requests whose `model` field mismatches, which removes the response-rewriting step llamacpp needs. The `--context` flag is passed only for the `llm` modality: asr/tts use small per-chunk defaults and a chat-sized window makes ASR crawl.

Transcription passes the client's `response_format` (and `temperature`) straight to the engine, because the engine implements that contract itself: `text` comes back as plain text, `json` and `verbose_json` as JSON — the latter with the engine's `task`, `language`, `duration` and `segments` — and any other value is refused with a client error naming it. So `srt`/`vtt` requests fail the same way they do on FLM rather than returning a transcript without timestamps.

A load that cannot start reports the way every other backend's does: the API answers `model_load_error` with status 500, and the diagnosis is in the message. Device loss is the case worth recognising — a subprocess that exits with status 75 before it reports ready names that in the load failure instead of a startup timeout, and one that exits 75 while serving is reaped by the watchdog and logged with its exit code, after which the next request reloads the model. Neither case gets a status of its own: like llama.cpp and vLLM, the diagnosis is in the message and the log rather than in the status, and the backend health state names `device_lost` only for as long as the backend object outlives the reset, which after a serving-time crash is until the router unloads it.

Gufo exits with code **75** when the HIP device enters the lost state; the load path and health state name this explicitly (`device_lost`) since reloading after GPU recovery is the only repair. A device supports at most ~4 concurrent HIP processes (8 compute queues), which aligns with the per-type LRU: at most one gufo process per model type can be loaded at once.

Chat entries pair a GGUF main checkpoint with a speculative companion (`draft`) plus a family label — `dflash` → `--speculative dflash2 --dflash-model`, `mtp` → `--mtp-model`, `dspark` → `--speculative dspark --dspark-model`. Sharded GGUFs (Flash-Next) resolve to the first shard path via the shared shard grouping; gufo discovers the sibling shards from it. Directory checkpoints (ASR/TTS/image) download the whole Hugging Face repo and pass the directory path.

**Engine twins.** A checkpoint the gufo catalog already names also served under another recipe — for example `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:UD-Q8_K_XL` registered with the `llamacpp` recipe — is mirrored as an `extra.<name>-Gufo` entry on the gufo recipe, so it can be selected for gufo from any client without re-registering or downloading again (the checkpoint cache is shared). The servable repositories are derived from the gufo catalog itself, so coverage grows exactly when the catalog does, and a twin is only offered when the engine can actually read that checkpoint: a downloaded artifact is judged tensor by tensor against the checkpoint table below, and before a download the catalog's declared variant must match (an unreadable sibling quant, such as a `UD-Q3_K_XL` whose experts are `IQ3_XXS`, gets no twin instead of a row that fails at load). Synthesis is additive (the source entry is untouched), generated ids are qualification-safe, and `engine_twins=false` in the runtime configuration suppresses it. The manual equivalent for a single model is `lemonade pull user.X --checkpoint <repo:variant> --recipe gufo`.

What the gate does not claim. A tensor whose name matches no declared group is accepted, because the engine validates only the tensors it loads — so a checkpoint carrying a group the table has not mirrored yet can pass the gate and still fail at load, and its load error stays the backstop. And because a twin copies its source's `draft` verbatim, a source whose speculative draft is quantized differently from what the engine expects yields a twin that cannot load — for Flash-Next, `mtp-…-Q4_K_M.gguf` is rejected while the catalog's `mtp-…-shared-Q8_0.gguf` loads. The catalog entry is the supported combination in such cases; a twin mirrors what the user registered.

**Checkpoint table.** `src/cpp/resources/gufo_compat.json` states which artifacts the engine can load, independently of the engine's source: one family per model architecture, each holding the tensor groups that architecture's loader distinguishes and the storage types each group accepts. A family claims repositories (`repos`), declares its speculative companions (`companions`: `dflash` points at `qwen38-dflash2`, whose tensor names differ from the host's in both directions, while `mtp` and `dspark` reuse the host's rules), and names the groups holding tensors the engine loads only under a configuration variant (`variant_groups` — audit metadata; the absence of a variant tensor is never a refusal). A group is its `exact` names, its `patterns` (`*` globs, nothing else), the accepted `types` spelled as the engine names them, and `mirrors`: the engine file and line range it was copied from. `block_divides_cols` marks the families whose loader additionally requires `columns % block_size(type) == 0`.

A verdict walks the tensors the artifact declares, takes the first group whose name rule matches (exact names before patterns, then declared array order — no inferred specificity), and rejects on the first type that group does not accept; a declared `draft` is judged under its companion's rules and ANDed in, so a servable main with an unreadable draft refuses the entry. Everything the table cannot decide answers *servable*: a repository no family claims, a tensor name no group claims, an unreadable header, and a table this binary cannot read (unknown schema, a type name the engine cannot print, a group with no names or no types). The last case logs one error and falls back to the flat "is this a type gufo implements at all" check, so a manifest that fell behind the engine hides nothing. A reject logs one line naming artifact, tensor, type, group and manifest stamp, which is what makes a withheld twin diagnosable from `lemonade logs` without attempting a load.

**Re-deriving a family from engine source.** Walk the loader's weight lookups, not its type enum: every `Get()`, role binding, `Layer()` and `Bind()` call site in that architecture's `weights.cpp`, reading the accepted-types expression at each. One expression becomes one group; two expressions never become one group, because the engine's per-site sets are not closed under union and a blended group accepts types that only one of its sites implements. Cite the expression's own range first (`mirrors: "src/models/qwen38_flash_next/weights.cpp:117-132"`), then the call sites that apply that same expression (`accepted at :244-282`). `test_gufo_compat --drift` requires the first range's `GgmlType::k…` tokens to equal the group's declared set and every later range's to be a subset, which is what catches a blend or a quietly widened range. Where the engine has no per-group whitelist at all — `deepseek-v4-flash` validates one flat decoder set — declare no groups, so the family accepts everything, which is the truth, rather than the table inventing a rule the loader does not have.

**When you bump gufo.** Two fields, two anchors. Move `engine.pin` to the release the image now bundles (`ARG GUFO_VERSION` in the `Dockerfile`); leave `engine.min_supported` where it is unless the re-read below shows a cited call site changed, and keep it equal to `kMinGufoVersion` in `src/cpp/include/lemon/backends/gufo/gufo.h` — a test asserts that, and the image smoke workflow asserts the pin against the bundled release. The floor is a claim about which releases this table is still correct for, so it moves only on evidence, never to match the pin. Then re-read every group against its cited range using the new checkout (`GUFO_SOURCE_DIR=/path/to/gufo ctest -R GufoCompatDrift`), pointed at the tag rather than a moving HEAD, and re-derive plus re-cite any group whose lines moved; if nothing moved, say so in the table's `_comment` and leave the groups alone. That command reports *skipped*, never passed, when no checkout is reachable, so a green CI run is not evidence that a re-diff happened. Re-earn the `pairings` rows whose evidence is that an engine loaded the artifact — that claim is about a release, so it has to name the release now bundled — while rows resting on a read or on the registry's intent carry over untouched. Re-check the groups named in each family's `variant_groups`, and keep `ctest -R GufoCompat` green: it judges the shipped table, its precedence golden list (`test/cpp/fixtures/gufo_compat/precedence.json`, 107 real tensor names, so reordering the array cannot silently move a name), and the registry cross-check.

**Pairings: what the registries actually ship.** The table's `pairings` section records every `main`/`draft` combination that `server_models.json` or the container seed declares, keyed by repository plus the registry checkpoint string *verbatim*. `repo:UD-Q4_K_XL` and `repo:Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` are two claims about two artifacts, and nothing resolves one into the other, because comparing them would need a download. Each row states the `evidence` behind it: `engine-loaded` (a gufo process loaded it), `inventory-measured` (the file was read and every tensor it declares fell inside the groups that claim it — `artifacts` names the files that were read), or `catalog-declared` (no artifact was reachable when the row was written, so it pins the strings and claims nothing else). `test_gufo_compat` cross-checks both registries against those rows without downloading weights: an entry whose draft differs from what was recorded fails even though its main alone would pass, and the rows the table excludes have to be the directory-shaped ones (transcription, TTS, image), so a chat entry cannot escape by spelling its `main` without a variant. `--drift --hub <dir>`, or `HF_HUB_CACHE`, additionally re-judges the entries whose files are cached and reports the rest as *not downloaded*. The gate never reads this section — it is a claim about the registry, enforced in CI — so a stale pairing row cannot change a verdict.

**Scope, and one gap left open on purpose.** The table governs entries whose recipe is `gufo` and nothing else: no other backend's resolution, download or load path consults it, and an artifact it refuses stays fully available to its own non-gufo entry. It also gates only *twin exposure* through `serves_model_checkpoint()`, so built-in rows stay pullable, listable and loadable whatever the table says; the worst a wrong row can cost is "a twin was not offered", never "a shipped model became uninstallable". Recorded here and deliberately left for its own change: `VLLMServer::load()` passes the canonical id to `--served-model-name`, so a namespaced `user.*` / `extra.*` entry would 404 against a strict engine. That is the same class of bug this gate exists to stop, on a backend this change does not touch.

### OpenMOSS (`openmoss`)

`moss-tts-server` hosts exactly one `--model` per process, so the voice generator that ships as a component of the speech model cannot be served by the same process. `OpenMossServer` runs the cascade one model at a time: the speech process is stopped, a transient process is spawned on the voice-generator checkpoint to render a single reference sample, and the speech process is brought back. Holding both would require a card that fits the pair, a strictly harder requirement than running the model that was actually asked for. For the same reason, `server_models.json` keeps `size` as the peak resident requirement of the main speech model rather than adding the non-resident VoiceGen download size. Rendered samples are cached per description for the life of the load, so repeating a description costs nothing. The speech process is restarted even when design fails, so an unsuccessful design cannot leave a loaded model with no process behind it.

The legacy `MOSS-VoiceGen` registry entry remains as a compatibility model for existing clients; integrated voice design on `OpenMOSS-TTS` and `MOSS-TTS-Local` does not depend on that standalone entry.

`request_mutex_` serialises a process-changing voice-design request against normal OpenMOSS inference, `load()`, and `unload()`. Speech and SFX hold it shared; voice design and lifecycle changes hold it exclusively. During the intentional speech -> VoiceGenerator -> speech swap, `process_swap_in_progress_` keeps `is_backend_alive()` true so the router does not mistake the temporarily empty speech-process handle for a crash. A request arriving in that window is accepted and then waits on `request_mutex_` until speech is restored. When the speech process fails its readiness wait, `start_server()` stops it, so the voice-design path does not call `unload()`, which would take the same exclusive lock again.

The transient design process is a local `NativeProcess` in `render_reference_sample()` rather than a `start_server()` call, because it does not own `port_`. Its readiness loop polls its own `/health` and checks `designer.running()` each round, so a subprocess that dies during model loading fails the request at once instead of polling to the deadline, and destroying `designer` stops the process and logs its exit code. `server_command()` picks the port with `find_free_port()` instead of `choose_port()` for the same reason: `choose_port()` assigns `port_`, and `start_server()` points `port_` at the speech process only.

Reference-conditioned TTS can exceed OpenMOSS's default 8192-token context. Lemonade intentionally keeps the upstream context default instead of forcing a larger allocation, preserving compatibility with memory-constrained GPUs. OpenMOSS v0.3 chunks prefill batches, but a complete prompt still has to fit `n_ctx`; unusually long references may therefore be rejected by upstream with guidance to shorten the reference or raise the context size.

Lemonade does not inject `max_audio_frames` into OpenMOSS speech requests. OpenMOSS v0.3 owns this policy: its VoiceGenerator derives a text-based duration window when needed, while MOSS-TTS/MOSS-TTSD keep their reference-aware/native stop behavior. Keeping that distinction in the backend avoids truncating conditioned or multi-speaker speech.

Voice design is opt-in through the `voice_design_description` extension and is never inferred from `voice`, which keeps its OpenAI-compatible meaning and is forwarded as an instruction. A client sending `"voice": "default"` gets speech rather than a design run for a voice literally named "default". The field is ignored when the request already carries `reference_wav_b64`. Request fields are read with a type-checking accessor rather than `json::value()`, which throws on a type mismatch instead of falling back to the default and would turn a client's wrong-typed field into a 500.

`MOSS-SoundEffect` uses the same recipe but is an audio-generation model: `audio_generations()` forwards to the backend's `/sfx` endpoint, accepting `duration`/`cfg` as aliases for `seconds`/`cfg_scale`.

### llama.cpp (`llamacpp`)

Lemonade launches `llama-server` with `--parallel 1` and leaves the upstream `--cache-ram` host prompt cache at its default. `LlamaCppServer` does not override `downsize()`: slot `erase` frees no device memory (the KV buffer is allocated once at model load) and discards the slot's KV state without going through the host-cache save path, so soft idle leaves the slot resident and a resumed conversation reuses its cached prefix.

### Model downloads

A checkpoint file can be reached twice during a registry download: once because the backend's `select_checkpoint_files` claimed it alongside the main weight, and again because it is also declared as its own checkpoint role (the OpenMOSS `.extras.gguf` sidecars are both). The same bytes either way, so `download_from_registry` collapses duplicates before counting, or the progress total overshoots.

### Backend auto-selection

When a recipe's backend is not pinned in `config.json` (the `backend` key is absent or `"auto"`), the default backend reported in `system-info` — and used by `RecipeOptions` when resolving `*_backend` options — is chosen as follows: the first supported backend in `RECIPE_DEFS` preference order wins, unless a later supported backend is already locally installed (state `installed`, `update_available`, or `update_required`) while the earlier candidates are merely installable. In that case the first installed one wins. This makes explicitly installing a variant (e.g. the Vulkan build of a GPU backend) an effective override: auto-selection uses what is on disk instead of downloading the preference-order winner. An explicit `backend` value in `config.json` always takes precedence over both rules. The llamacpp `system` variant is never auto-selected unless `prefer_system` is set.
